clips.send: Theory says heads should come up half the time. Let’s really flip a coin 10 times. 7 heads! The experimental probability is 7 over 10 equals 0.7 , not 0.5. Is the theory wrong?
clips.text: Theory says heads should come up half the time. Let’s really flip a coin 10 times... 7 heads! The experimental probability is over 7 10 = 0.7, not 0.5. Is the theory wrong?

clips.send: Roll two dice. A 6 by 6 table shows all 36 equally likely outcomes. A total of 7 can happen in 6 ways, more than any other total, so P(7) equals 6 over 36 equals 1 over 6 . A total of 2 happens in only 1 way.
clips.text: Roll two dice. A 6 by 6 table shows all 36 equally likely outcomes. A total of 7 can happen in 6 ways, more than any other total, so P(7) = over 6 36 = over 16. A total of 2 happens in only 1 way.

clips.send: A fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes. Three of them are even: 2, 4 and 6. So the probability of rolling an even number is 3 over 6 equals 1 over 2 . Count the favourable outcomes, then divide by all the equally likely outcomes.
clips.text: A fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes. Three of them are even: 2, 4 and 6. So the probability of rolling an even number is over 3 6 = over 12. Count the favourable outcomes, then divide by all the equally likely outcomes.

clips.send: Flip two coins. A tree diagram lists every outcome: HH, HT, TH and TT, four equally likely outcomes. One head and one tail happens in two of them, so its probability is 2 over 4 equals 1 over 2 , not 1 over 3 .
clips.text: Flip two coins. A tree diagram lists every outcome: HH, HT, TH and TT, four equally likely outcomes. One head and one tail happens in two of them, so its probability is over 24 = over 12, not over 13.

clips.send: Probability helps us predict. Roll a die 600 times: we expect each number about 600 times 1 over 6 equals 100 times. The real counts land close to 100, but rarely exactly on it.
clips.text: Probability helps us predict. Roll a die 600 times: we expect each number about 600 times over 16 = 100 times. The real counts land close to 100, but rarely exactly on it.

clips.send: Keep flipping: 100, 1000, then 10,000 times. At first the fraction of heads jumps around, but as the flips pile up it settles closer and closer to 0.5. This is the law of large numbers: with many trials, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability.
clips.text: Keep flipping: 100, 1000, then 10,000 times. At first the fraction of heads jumps around, but as the flips pile up it settles closer and closer to 0.5. This is the law of large numbers: with many trials, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability.

clips.send: A bag holds 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green marbles. P(blue) equals 5 over 10 equals 1 over 2 and P(not red) equals 1 minus 3 over 10 equals 7 over 10 . Draw 200 times, putting the marble back each time, and expect about 200 times 1 over 2 equals 100 blues.
clips.text: A bag holds 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green marbles. P( text blue ) = over 5 10 = over 12 and P( text not red ) = 1 - over 3 10 = over 7 10 . Draw 200 times, putting the marble back each time, and expect about 200 times over 12 = 100 blues.

clips.send: Probability measures how likely something is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Rolling a 7 on a normal die is impossible, a coin landing heads is an even chance, 1 over 2 , and rolling a number from 1 to 6 is certain.
clips.text: Probability measures how likely something is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Rolling a 7 on a normal die is impossible, a coin landing heads is an even chance, over 12, and rolling a number from 1 to 6 is certain.

clips.send: The key ideas: every probability is between 0 and 1. With equally likely outcomes, P equals favourable over total . And the chance that something does not happen is 1 minus P : for example, the probability of not rolling a 6 is 1 minus 1 over 6 equals 5 over 6 .
clips.text: The key ideas: every probability is between 0 and 1. With equally likely outcomes, P = over text favourable text total . And the chance that something does not happen is 1 - P: for example, the probability of not rolling a 6 is 1 - over 16 = over 56.

clips.send: 抛两枚硬币。用树状图列出所有结果：正正、正反、反正、反反，共 4 种等可能的结果。“一正一反”占其中 2 种，所以它的概率是 4分之2 等于 2分之1 ，而不是 3分之1 。
clips.text: 抛两枚硬币。用树状图列出所有结果：正正、正反、反正、反反，共 4 种等可能的结果。“一正一反”占其中 2 种，所以它的概率是 over 24 = over 12，而不是 over 13。

clips.send: 一个均匀的骰子有 6 种等可能的结果，其中 3 种是偶数：2、4、6。所以掷出偶数的概率是 6分之3 等于 2分之1 。数出有利结果的个数，再除以所有等可能结果的个数。
clips.text: 一个均匀的骰子有 6 种等可能的结果，其中 3 种是偶数：2、4、6。所以掷出偶数的概率是 over 3 6 = over 12。数出有利结果的个数，再除以所有等可能结果的个数。

clips.send: 概率用 0 到 1 之间的数表示事件发生的可能性有多大：0 表示不可能，1 表示必然发生。用普通骰子掷出 7 是不可能的；硬币正面朝上是一半一半，即 2分之1 ；掷出 1 到 6 中的某个数是必然的。
clips.text: 概率用 0 到 1 之间的数表示事件发生的可能性有多大：0 表示不可能，1 表示必然发生。用普通骰子掷出 7 是不可能的；硬币正面朝上是一半一半，即 over 12；掷出 1 到 6 中的某个数是必然的。

clips.send: 理论上，正面朝上应该占一半。我们真的抛 10 次……得到 7 次正面！实验概率（频率）是 10分之7 等于 0.7 ，而不是 0.5。难道理论错了吗？
clips.text: 理论上，正面朝上应该占一半。我们真的抛 10 次……得到 7 次正面！实验概率（频率）是 over 7 10 = 0.7，而不是 0.5。难道理论错了吗？

clips.send: 继续抛：100 次、1000 次，再到 10000 次。开始时正面的频率上下跳动，但随着次数越来越多，它越来越稳定地靠近 0.5。这就是大数定律：试验次数很多时，实验概率（频率）会接近理论概率。
clips.text: 继续抛：100 次、1000 次，再到 10000 次。开始时正面的频率上下跳动，但随着次数越来越多，它越来越稳定地靠近 0.5。这就是大数定律：试验次数很多时，实验概率（频率）会接近理论概率。

clips.send: 关键结论：概率都在 0 到 1 之间。结果等可能时，概率 等于 有利结果数 除以 所有结果数。事件不发生的概率是 1 减 P ：例如，掷出的不是 6 的概率是 1 减 6分之1 等于 6分之5 。
clips.text: 关键结论：概率都在 0 到 1 之间。结果等可能时，概率 = 有利结果数 ÷ 所有结果数。事件不发生的概率是 1 - P：例如，掷出的不是 6 的概率是 1 - over 16 = over 56。

clips.send: 概率可以用来预测。把骰子掷 600 次：每个点数预计出现约 600 乘 6分之1 等于 100 次。实际次数都接近 100，但很少正好是 100。
clips.text: 概率可以用来预测。把骰子掷 600 次：每个点数预计出现约 600 times over 16 = 100 次。实际次数都接近 100，但很少正好是 100。

clips.send: 袋子里有 3 个红球、5 个蓝球、2 个绿球。摸到蓝球的概率是 10分之5 等于 2分之1 ，摸到的不是红球的概率是 1 减 10分之3 等于 10分之7 。摸 200 次（每次摸完放回），预计约有 200 乘 2分之1 等于 100 次摸到蓝球。
clips.text: 袋子里有 3 个红球、5 个蓝球、2 个绿球。摸到蓝球的概率是 over 5 10 = over 12，摸到的不是红球的概率是 1 - over 3 10 = over 7 10 。摸 200 次（每次摸完放回），预计约有 200 times over 12 = 100 次摸到蓝球。
